surfaces.part: snow-capped fir tree (stacked conical foliage tiers with snow tip)

answer.evidence: The fir is drawn as a conical silhouette of stacked foliage tiers. The width profile grows steadily from 4 at row 15 to 28 at rows 58-60, with small notches at rows 29, 39-40 and 49-50 where one tier ends and the next begins. These tiers are shaded dark-to-light bands. No horizontal ellipse or top plane is drawn. The snow at rows 16-22 is the tip of the cone, and the snow patches at rows 42-43 and 53-54 are small highlights on branch edges, not top surfaces. For an organic object like a tree, a conical elevation is acceptable, but under the measurement rules there is no top surface (main_top_rows 0). The form reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small snow-laden fir with scalloped tiers. Its green ramp has about 4 steps, from deep teal-green shadow under each tier to lighter green, plus white and pale snow caps on the tiers and the tip. That makes about 5 steps overall, close to the references. Edges are a dark, tinted green with no neutral black line (0% near-neutral dark edge pixels, same as both references), and forms are separated by value. There are no flat fills (0% near-flat coverage). Snow clumps and green speckle on the tiers give some grain. The measured 12 visible tones per tile sit between tree-1a786c (7) and tree-d43edd (29). The fir is smaller and simpler than the big leafy tree, so it reads slightly less dense than that one, but it is at least as rich as the other reference and does not look like a flat sticker. A careful artist would accept it next to the references.
